headline: Jay Rockefeller, Senate voice on health care and security, dies at 89
author: Louie Estrada

paragraphs.text: John D. “Jay” Rockefeller IV, an heir to a vast oil fortune and a liberal Democrat who entered politics in his adopted home state of West Virginia, serving as governor and a five-term U.S. senator and becoming a leading voice on health care, tax reform, social welfare and national security, died Friday at his home in Washington, D.C. He was 89. His family did not provide a cause.

Mr. Rockefeller was a great-grandson of billionaire industrialist John D. Rockefeller Sr., whose Standard Oil Trust monopolized the oil industry in the early 20th century and made him one of the world’s richest people.

Rockefeller descendants have figured prominently in philanthropy, business and politics. Mr. Rockefeller’s father was philanthropist John D. Rockefeller III; one uncle, Nelson A. Rockefeller, was elected governor of New York four times before being appointed vice president of the United States; another uncle, Winthrop Rockefeller, was elected governor of Arkansas twice; and yet another, David Rockefeller Sr., rose to become chairman and chief executive of Chase Manhattan Bank.

Having grown up a blue-blooded Northeasterner, Mr. Rockefeller made an unlikely public face of West Virginia. The rugged Appalachian state, long dependent on the coal industry, was beset by troubles: an aging population, high poverty, low-performing schools and a stagnant job market dominated by low-wage jobs.

Arriving on Capitol Hill in 1985, after two terms as governor, Mr. Rockefeller worked in the shadow of West Virginia’s long-serving senior senator, Democrat Robert C. Byrd, while burrowing deep into committee work and distinguishing himself as an earnest and dogged advocate for society’s most vulnerable.

His signature accomplishments included expanding eligibility of the earned income tax credit and establishing the child tax credit and the Children’s Health Insurance Program, a federal-state initiative that provides health coverage to children in low-income families. He also worked to protect Medicare, the federal health insurance program for the elderly and disabled, from proposed budget cuts.

Beginning in the late 1980s, he chaired a bipartisan commission established by Congress to study health coverage and long-term care. He was a key supporter in 1993 of the unsuccessful effort led by then-first lady Hillary Clinton to create a national system of universal health care. After that, he voted for and defended the Affordable Care Act, a step toward universal coverage that President Barack Obama signed into law in 2010.

Mr. Rockefeller successfully sponsored legislation to expand research into and treatment of illnesses related to military service. And, of particular interest to many West Virginians, he had a hand in writing legislation to protect the health benefits of coal miners and their families after mining companies shuttered operations. He was also a sponsor of 2006 legislation that updated mine-safety regulations.

Broadband internet access in rural communities and computer security were among Mr. Rockefeller’s other long-standing concerns. In one of his final legislative efforts, he sponsored the Cybersecurity Enhancement Act of 2014. The bill established a public-private partnership to set security standards and promote research and development aimed at protecting computer systems and networks involved in the operation of critical infrastructure.

Mr. Rockefeller, at various times, chaired the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation, the Veterans’ Affairs Committee and the Intelligence Committee. In 2008, he led a bipartisan Senate investigation into the lead-up to the Iraq War. The committee report concluded that President George W. Bush’s administration had misrepresented intelligence on Iraq to justify the military invasion in 2003.

“There’s always talk in the Senate that members are either workhorses or showhorses,” said Donald A. Ritchie, historian emeritus of the U.S. Senate, in a 2022 interview for this obituary. “A showhorse is a senator who is on TV all the time. The workhorses — like Rockefeller — aren’t seen as much because they are in the committee doing the nitty-gritty work.”

Although Mr. Rockefeller voted with his Democratic colleagues more than 90 percent of the time, he wasn’t seen as ideological or partisan. “He was able to work with friends he made across the aisle,” Ritchie said.
Getting to know West Virginia

Mr. Rockefeller arrived in West Virginia as an idealistic 27-year-old community organizer with Volunteers in Service to America (VISTA), an anti-poverty program established by President Lyndon B. Johnson. The group required volunteers to take an oath of poverty before they went to live with host families in impoverished communities, mostly in the South and Appalachia.

His assignment sent him to Emmons, a remote mining town on the Big Coal River, about 20 miles south of Charleston, the state capital. It took months for townspeople to warm up to the 6-foot-6 stranger whose surname evoked a history of violent labor struggles in the early 20th century.

In Emmons, Mr. Rockefeller focused on youth and health care projects. He started the town’s first Little League team, led the construction of a community center and organized a mobile health-screening service for women.

Mr. Rockefeller decided to stay in West Virginia after his assignment ended, and then he began to climb the local political ladder — not as a Republican, in line with family tradition, but as a Democrat. His choice of political affiliation made national news at a time when “Rockefeller Republican” was shorthand for membership in the party’s moderate wing.

As a member of one of America’s most prominent families, much of his life was chronicled in the press. His 1967 marriage to Sharon Percy, daughter of U.S. Sen. Charles H. Percy (R-Illinois), made the cover of Life magazine. The next year, Mr. Rockefeller got a call from his uncle Nelson, then New York governor, offering to appoint him to the Senate seat of Robert F. Kennedy (D-New York), who had been assassinated while running for president.
“I said no immediately,” Mr. Rockefeller told The Washington Post years later, adding that he had ambitions of serving in the Senate but didn’t want the job handed to him.
Mr. Rockefeller served in the state House of Delegates from 1966 to 1968 and then was secretary of state through 1972, when he made an unsuccessful run for governor.

In the only political defeat of his career, he lost to Republican incumbent Arch Moore Jr., who accused Mr. Rockefeller of seeking to destroy the coal industry after the Democratic candidate called for a ban on strip mining, which has been linked to such problems as soil erosion and stream pollution.

For much of his career, Mr. Rockefeller’s political opponents derided him as a Yankee carpetbagger, an opportunistic outsider with deep pockets and a deeper sense of privilege. Moore ran TV ads that asked, “How’d you like to have a governor of New York from West Virginia?”

After losing the 1972 race, Mr. Rockefeller spent about four years as president of West Virginia Wesleyan College in Buckhannon before winning the first of two terms as governor in 1976. By that time, he had won over coal miners by reversing his stance on strip mining, reasoning that mining companies had taken steps to address environmental concerns.
During his tenure as governor, Mr. Rockefeller emphasized government ethics, affordable housing and infrastructure projects. He created the state’s first board of coal mine health and safety.

He was elected to the Senate in 1984, replacing Sen. Jennings Randolph (D), who was retiring. In 2013, Mr. Rockefeller announced his retirement from the Senate ahead of the 2014 election, which was won by Shelley Moore Capito (R), daughter of former governor Moore.

Survivors include his wife, Sharon Percy Rockefeller, the president and chief executive of WETA, Washington’s public broadcasting station; four children, John D. Rockefeller V, Valerie Rockefeller, Charles Rockefeller and Justin Aldrich Rockefeller; and nine grandchildren.
Elite schools and the Far East

John Rockefeller was born in Manhattan on June 18, 1937. He was one of four children and the only son of John D. Rockefeller III and the former Blanchette Ferry Hooker. His parents didn’t put the middle name Davison or the roman numeral suffix on his birth certificate, intending to spare him what they worried might be a burden.

“As a boy,” he told Life, “I was told that I should make up my own mind whether I wanted to carry on the full name, which I think stands for public service, a sense of responsibility, and a high standard of demand on oneself. When I was 21, I wrote a letter to my father saying I wanted the name and the responsibility.”

Amid the opulence of his youth — including a 3,000-acre family estate in suburban Westchester County — Jay Rockefeller had a strict Baptist upbringing. Idleness was considered a sin. If he wished to speak with his father, he had to schedule an appointment in the family study.

He graduated in 1954 from Phillips Exeter Academy boarding school, then majored in Far Eastern languages and history at Harvard. He had developed an affinity for Asian culture on family trips to Japan. But by his junior year, he desperately wanted to leave what he called his “privileged surroundings” and what looked to be the preordained trajectory of his life into the Northeast Republican establishment.

With the help of a sympathetic professor, Mr. Rockefeller obtained a temporary position teaching English at International Christian University in Tokyo. He lived with a group of Japanese students in a wood and paper shack in the middle of a rice field. During school breaks, he visited his friends’ families, many of whom worked on farms, struggling to rebuild their lives in the aftermath of World War II.

“It was a very personal experience for me, a very deep experience. It was the beginning of putting me on the track to public service,” Mr. Rockefeller said in the 2015 public television documentary “Jay: A Rockefeller’s Journey.”

He returned to Harvard in 1960, received a bachelor’s degree the next year and joined the nascent Peace Corps as special assistant to R. Sargent Shriver, its founding director. He also worked briefly for the State Department’s East Asian division.

But he grew restless in desk jobs and yearned to participate in grassroots community work. Through Action for Appalachian Youth, a program affiliated with VISTA, he traveled to West Virginia in 1964 on a one-year assignment to do social work in Emmons, where most of 250 residents relied on government assistance for food.
In the small town, he found a cause and a mission.
“My time there was transformative,” Mr. Rockefeller said in his 2014 farewell speech to the Senate. “It explains every policy I have pursued and every vote I have cast.”

correctionA previous version of this article incorrectly stated that Mr. Rockefeller's wife, Sharon Percy Rockefeller, was the former president and chief executive of WETA, Washington’s public broadcasting station. She still holds those positions.
